title: Pornography: Men Possessing Women
author: Andrea Dworkin
target_audience: Students and academics in gender studies and cultural studies
Individuals seeking critical perspectives on sex, media, and gender
core_themes: Pornography as a form of violence and oppression against women
Sexual politics and the institutionalization of male dominance
Intersection of sexuality, power, and objectification
Connections between pornography, rape, and broader societal misogyny
Role of law and liberalism in perpetuating exploitation
primary_purpose: To critically examine pornography as both a symbol and instrument of male domination, arguing that it perpetuates violence against women and shapes oppressive sexual politics within culture and society.

structure_format.organization: Structured into essays, case studies, and critical commentary, including historical and literary analysis
features: Direct citations from pornography and legal/academic sources
Critical analysis of liberal and sexual liberation discourses

key_concepts_lessons: Pornography is not simply expression, but a practice and ideology that legitimizes violence against women.
Sexual representation must be understood in terms of power and institutional arrangements, not just individual freedom or choice.
Sexual freedom for women is not achievable within structures that eroticize domination and subordination.
Legal and free speech arguments often fail to account for the harms and realities of sexual exploitation.
Society tolerates sexual abuse, objectification, and even violence, so long as it is framed as sexual entertainment.
notable_features: Influential in second-wave feminist anti-pornography activism
Groundbreaking for its time and shaped legal and academic debates
Combines personal testimony, statistics, and theoretical argument
Frequently cited, often polarizing within feminist scholarship
cultural_historical_context: Published during the early 1980s, amid the rise of the second-wave feminist movement and a growing anti-pornography campaign led by feminist writers like Andrea Dworkin and Catharine MacKinnon. The book emerged during intense debates about sexuality, censorship, freedom of expression, and the sexual revolution.
reception_impact: Seminal and controversial within feminism, generating strong support and equally strong criticism
Prompted the drafting of model anti-pornography ordinances and influenced legal scholarship
Frequently cited in debates on pornography, censorship, and women's rights
Criticized by some for conflating pornography with all expressions of sexuality and for its perceived lack of nuance
Regarded as a foundational text in radical feminist critique of pornography
comparable_titles: Only Words by Catharine A. MacKinnon
Against Our Will: Men, Women and Rape by Susan Brownmiller
